cover.headline: India's best-run value grocer, now growing at ~15% with quick commerce at the metro gates: fairly priced after the retail de-rating
cover.lead: DMart runs 503 owned-or-leased hypermarkets (20.7 mn sq ft) selling food, FMCG and general merchandise at everyday low prices, plus a loss-making online arm (DMart Ready). Q1FY27 showed the new shape of growth: standalone revenue +15.1% on ~19% more selling area, like-for-like growth down to 5.5% (older metro stores flat), consolidated profit +11%. Management's plan is to add ~15% to the store base a year and keep gross margin at 14-15%. We forecast EPS of ₹50.9 / ₹59.9 / ₹71.5 for FY27-29E. The street's targets are DCF, EV/EBITDA or P/E, but every note translates into a **one-year-forward P/E** (54-65x). The house rule (DMart's forward P/E median since 2021, 88.4x, cut by the 30.2% de-rating of listed retailers) gives **61.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹65.7 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD**. Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹3,657; DCF only ₹989. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: 500 stores at Mar-26 after a record 85 openings in FY26 (58 in Q4), and a 2-3 year pipeline of land. Management's internal benchmark is ~15% more stores a year; we model 75 / 85 / 95 openings for FY27-29E (755 stores, 30.8 mn sq ft by FY29E). New stores in Tier 1-2 towns ramp well; land, not capital or people, is the bottleneck.

arguments.h: But each sq ft is earning less
arguments.p: Same-store growth fell from ~10% in FY24 to ~8% in FY26 and 5.5% in Q1FY27. Dense metro stores are full and losing small baskets to Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto, Flipkart Minutes and Amazon Now, whose prices are now within 4-13% of DMart's (Emkay). Our revenue per effective sq ft falls 2.5% in FY27E and grows only 1-1.5% after that.

arguments.h: A fixed margin and heavier capital
arguments.p: EBITDA margin stays in its 7.5-8% band by choice; growth below EBITDA is slower as depreciation, lease interest and new borrowings rise (₹965 cr of commercial paper at Mar-26, ~₹2,000 cr expected by Mar-27). DMart Ready lost ₹307 cr in FY26 and has retreated to 11 cities. ROE is ~13%, against 18-20% before Covid.

At ₹3,801 DMart trades at 63.5x our FY28E and 57.9x Sep-28E EPS, below its 88.4x median since 2021 but in line with what the de-rated sector justifies. Listed retailers were 30.2% below their five-year P/E medians on 30-Sep-2026. Our {{dcf.tp|inr}} is close to the post-Q1 street median (₹4,058). A DCF at an 11% cost of capital supports barely a quarter of the price: the stock pays for decades of growth in advance.

catalysts: Q2FY27 business update (early October) and results (due by mid-October 2026): store openings in H1 (5 by 28-Jul) against a ~75-store year, and whether like-for-like growth recovers from 5.5%.
Festive season and FMCG price increases: DMart passes inflation straight through, so pricing helps revenue per sq ft in H2.
DMart Ready after the exit from 7 cities: whether the loss (₹75 cr in Q1FY27) narrows in H2FY27.
Quick commerce in Tier 2 towns: Blinkit, Instamart and Zepto expanding into the next 50-100 cities where most new DMart stores open.
Funding: the ₹1,000 cr NCD and commercial paper; borrowings to ~₹2,000 cr by Mar-27.

sections.title: A no-frills hypermarket chain that wins on price: owned stores, fast vendor payment, a 14-15% gross margin

blocks.p: DMart sells everyday goods at the lowest prices it can sustain: foods (staples, dairy, snacks, fruit and vegetables; 57.9% of FY26 revenue), non-food FMCG (home and personal care; 19.82%) and general merchandise and apparel (kitchenware, plastics, home textiles, garments; 22.28%). Its formula is "everyday low cost, everyday low price": it owns most of its stores (no rent escalation), runs simple formats of ~40,000 sq ft, pays suppliers in about a week in return for better terms, and passes savings to shoppers rather than to margin. The result is a gross margin of only ~14-15% and an EBITDA margin of ~8%, on very high sales per sq ft (₹33,422 in FY26 on year-end area).

At Mar-26 it had 500 stores and 20.6 mn sq ft in 17 states and union territories, still concentrated in the west and south: Maharashtra 128, Gujarat 75, Karnataka 50, Telangana 48, Andhra Pradesh 47, Tamil Nadu 35; 68 stores are on long leases. 398 mn bills were cut in FY26 (average bill ~₹1,683, HSIE). The listed company (standalone) is the store business: ₹66,968 cr of revenue and ₹5,255 cr of EBITDA (7.8%). The subsidiaries add ₹1,853 cr of revenue net of intra-group sales: DMart Ready (Avenue E-Commerce, online grocery, ₹4,094 cr of sales, EBITDA −₹185 cr), Align Retail Trades (packing, ₹3,871 cr, mostly sold to DMart) and Avenue Food Plaza (in-store food counters, ₹307 cr).

sections.title: From one Mumbai store in 2002 to 500: two equity raises, no dividends, no acquisitions

blocks.p: Radhakishan Damani, a stock-market investor, founded Avenue Supermarts in 2000 and opened the first DMart in Mumbai in 2002. The chain grew slowly and profitably in Maharashtra and Gujarat before listing in 2017; since then it has entered the south, central and north India in clusters. There have been no acquisitions, demergers or bonus issues; the share count rose only through the 2020 QIP and employee stock options, so per-share history needs no adjustment.

The 2026 CEO change was planned: Anshul Asawa became CEO on 1-Feb-2026 when Ignatius Navil Noronha completed his tenure, after what Mr Asawa called a well-planned transition year spent in stores and distribution centres.

sections.title: Indian retail: a ₹112 trn market, only ~13% organised, and a new channel growing far faster than stores

blocks.p: Indian retail ~Rs112 trn in FY26 (+~10%); organised retail ~Rs15 trn (+15%, ~13% of the total); e-retail ~Rs5.5 trn (+16%, ~4.9%); food and grocery ~32% of organised retail; retail to grow 9.7-10.4% a year over 2025-30 (CRISIL Research, cited in AR FY26 MD&A). ~1.5% of Indian retail; DMart's categories cover only ~50% of the retail wallet (Emkay initiation, 12-Apr-2026).

bullets: **Quick commerce is the new competitor.** Quick commerce (Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto, Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now) is already ~1.5x modern trade in key metros (Emkay estimate) and is moving into the next 50-100 cities. Emkay's monthly-basket check: QC prices only 4-13% above DMart stores before bank offers, similar or lower after them. Blinkit runs at 25-26% gross margin vs DMart's 14-15%; dark stores turn inventory ~10x faster per store than DMart's ~2x (Emkay). DMart management (28-Jul-2026): more players than last year; some small baskets move to QC for convenience and this 'is not going to change over the next few years'; FMCG vendors still doubling down on DMart, often its largest single customer.

**Metros vs smaller towns.** Older, dense metro stores (Mumbai, Bangalore) are near capacity; DMart opens nearby stores, cannibalising same-store growth. Tier 1-2 stores ramp better and grow faster (management, 28-Jul-2026). Emkay and Goldman Sachs: older large-metro stores flat y/y in Q1FY27.

**Other formats.** Reliance Retail's Smart Bazaar and Vishal Mega Mart (listed Dec-2024) are the large store-based rivals Emkay tracks; Amazon (Amazon Now) and Flipkart (Flipkart Minutes) compete online and in quick commerce. Management says FMCG vendors are doubling down on DMart, often their largest single customer.

**Pricing is set by MRP.** Packaged goods carry a printed maximum retail price, so shoppers compare discounts easily; DMart's edge is the depth of the discount across a whole basket, not a cheaper product (CEO, 28-Jul-2026).

blocks.callout: **What matters for DMart:** organised retail still has decades of runway, but the share of that runway that goes to large-format stores is no longer obvious. Quick commerce has taken the convenience basket in metros in under three years; whether it can take the monthly stock-up basket, and how fast it reaches Tier 2 towns, decides DMart's same-store growth.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the consumption and formalisation tailwind reaches DMart through new stores; it no longer lifts the old stores much. The fastest channel shift in Indian grocery (quick commerce) runs against DMart in its densest markets, so the company has to grow by building more stores, which is slower and more capital-hungry than growing sales in the ones it has.

sections.title: The store engine: area grows ~15-20% a year, but each sq ft now earns less than it did in FY24

blocks.p: DMart grows in clusters: it enters a state, builds density, then moves on (five new states in FY26, mostly in the north). Openings depend on land: DMart prefers to buy, takes 2-3 years from purchase to opening, and keeps a 2-3 year pipeline. Management's internal benchmark is to add ~15% of the store base a year, "a few percentages higher or lower" depending on approvals; FY26 was 20% (85 stores) because sites finished early, and 58 of them opened in Q4. Q1FY27 added only 3 (2 more by 28-Jul). Leasing is now used where land is hard to buy (NCR): 15 of FY26's 85 stores were leased.

The other half of the equation is productivity. Our measure, standalone revenue per average sq ft, rose from ₹28,659 in FY21 (Covid) to ₹34,760 in FY24, then flattened: ₹35,783 in FY25 and ₹35,433 in FY26 (the company's own measure on year-end area fell from ₹33,896 to ₹33,422). Three things drag it: like-for-like growth slowed from ~10% (FY24) to 8.1% (FY26) and 5.5% in Q1FY27 as dense metro stores hit capacity and lose small baskets to quick commerce; DMart deliberately opens stores next to crowded ones, cannibalising them; and new stores in Tier 2-3 towns start well below the system average and take years to ramp (management did not disclose by how much).

sections.title: DMart Ready: ₹4,094 cr of sales, a ₹307 cr loss and a retreat to 11 cities

blocks.p: Avenue E-Commerce runs DMart Ready, an online grocery service built for large planned baskets: slotted delivery within six hours (and pick-up points, now de-emphasised) at DMart prices. Sales grew 17% to ₹4,094 cr in FY26, but the loss widened: EBITDA −₹185 cr (−₹129 cr in FY25), net loss ₹307 cr (₹247 cr). DMart has injected ~₹1,488 cr of equity into it to date (HSIE). The CEO was blunt on 28-Jul-2026: as the business spread to more cities "our losses also grew quite significantly", so it has left 7 cities where order density was too low (25 cities in FY25, 18 in FY26, 11 now) and will try to prove a profitable six-hour model there first. It will not run a quick-commerce model and will not merge the online business into the stores.

Q1FY27 shows the cost of the retreat: on the consolidated-less-standalone proxy, revenue grew ~5% (vs ~20% a year earlier) and the loss rose to ~₹75.3 cr (₹56.9 cr in Q1FY26, ₹68.2 cr in Q4FY26; Nuvama, Citi). We assume the subsidiaries' revenue grows 5% / 8% / 10% and their EBITDA improves from −₹66 cr in FY26 to −₹60 cr / −₹30 cr / ₹0 cr in FY27-29E.

blocks.callout: **So what:** DMart Ready is ~6% of group sales and costs ~₹4-5 a share of profit a year. It is not a growth option the market should pay for until the 11-city model shows a path to break-even; it matters mainly as evidence of how hard it is for DMart to follow its customers online.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** DMart has a real, wide moat in what it does: running low-cost stores for planned grocery shopping. Nobody in India has matched its cost per rupee of sales, and its returns (~13% ROE with no leverage) are earned, not borrowed. The moat does not extend to convenience, which is where Indian grocery is shifting fastest in the big cities. The question for the stock is not whether DMart survives quick commerce (it will) but whether same-store growth settles at 5-8% instead of 10%+.

sections.title: Revenue 2.8x in six years at a steady ~8% EBITDA margin; profit growth has lagged since FY23

blocks.p: DMart's consolidated revenue was ₹24,870 cr in FY20 and ₹68,821 cr in FY26 (18.5% a year), almost all from new stores: retail area went from 7.8 mn to 20.6 mn sq ft. The EBITDA margin is remarkably stable, 7.2-9.0% since FY18, because DMart chooses to hand cost savings back to customers (gross margin is held at 14-15%). What has changed is the line below EBITDA: depreciation rose from ₹639 cr in FY23 to ₹1,037 cr in FY26 and finance cost doubled in FY26 (more leased stores, first commercial paper), while other income fell as cash was spent. So net profit grew only 7.7% a year over FY23-26 against revenue growth of 17.1%. FY23 and FY25 profit include one-off tax gains of ₹138.8 cr and ₹36.0 cr.

pair.title: Depreciation and finance cost are rising faster than revenue

blocks.callout: **Our view:** DMart is a volume machine with a fixed margin. Growth comes from opening stores, not from squeezing more out of each rupee of sales. That is a strength (customers trust the prices) and a limit: when same-store growth slows and new stores take longer to ramp, profit growth cannot be rescued by margin, and the rising cost of owning and now leasing stores shows up below EBITDA.

bullets: **Growth:** standalone revenue +15.1% on ~19% more average selling area: revenue per sq ft fell ~3%. LFL 5.5% (7.1% a year earlier); older large-metro stores flat (Emkay, Goldman Sachs); bills per store −4.4%, average bill +1.5% (Elara); GM&A +19% (Emkay). March pantry-loading flattered Q4FY26 (LFL 10.8%) and spilled into Q1 (CEO).

**Margins:** gross margin up ~50bp y/y to a multi-quarter high, but staff cost +30%+ (capability build, the wage code from Dec-2025) left the EBITDA margin up only ~10bp (JPMorgan, Jefferies). Depreciation +24% and finance cost +86% (leases, commercial paper) held PBT growth to ~12%.

**Guidance (analyst meet, 28-Jul-2026):** Internal benchmark: add ~15% of the store base each year; a few points higher or lower depending on land and approvals (MD & CEO, 28-Jul-2026). 2-3 year pipeline of sites; land to store takes 2-3 years. Open to long leases (NCR) and stores under 40,000 sq ft. Gross margin 14-15% and net margin ~5%; savings passed to customers; staff cost built 'ahead of the curve'. Same-store growth for older stores to hover around last year's level (~8%); metro stores near saturation, some loss of small baskets to quick commerce expected to persist.
**DMart Ready:** Focus on 11 cities with 6-hour slotted delivery for large baskets; no quick-commerce model; aim to cut losses significantly; no merger with the store business.
**Funding:** Borrowings may reach ~Rs2,000 cr by Mar-27 (CP plus a Rs1,000 cr NCD) to fund capex; capex 'upwards of Rs4,000 cr' in FY26.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Q1 confirmed that DMart is now a ~15% grower, not a ~20% one: area growth of 15-20% minus a few points of productivity dilution. The margin is steady, but profit grows slower than revenue because of depreciation and interest. Our FY27E assumes 75 openings, most in H2.

sections.title: Every rupee goes into stores: capex now exceeds operating cash, and returns have drifted down to ~13% ROE

blocks.p: DMart buys the land and builds most of its stores (only 68 of 500 were leased at Mar-26). That keeps rent out of the P&L and prices low, but it ties up capital: ₹6,074 cr of capex in FY18-21 and ₹14,889 cr in FY22-26 against ₹12,678 cr of operating cash in FY22-26. FY26 capex was ₹4,113 cr (FY25 ₹3,423 cr), and ₹5,294 cr of contracts for sites under construction were still to be paid at Mar-26 (₹4,299 cr a year earlier). It has never paid a dividend; the two equity raises (IPO 2017, QIP 2020) funded the land bank until FY25. ROE fell from 16.0% in FY23 to 12.9% in FY26; management's own ROCE (EBIT on capital employed net of cash) was 17.1% in FY26.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** DMart's model is capital-hungry: FY26 capex of ₹4,113 cr was ~₹48 cr per store opened (it also buys land 2-3 years ahead), and a new store takes years to reach full throughput. At ~15% store growth a year, capex runs ahead of cash and debt rises (management: ~₹2,000 cr of borrowings by Mar-27). We model ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}} for FY27-29E: positive economics, but no longer the 18-20% of the pre-Covid years.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean, simple accounts; two small tax one-offs; profit converts well to cash

bullets: **Cash conversion is good.** Cash from operations (after tax) was ₹3,467 cr in FY26 against EBITDA of ₹5,189 cr (67%), after ₹856 cr more inventory as distribution centres were added. Customers pay at the till (receivables ~1 day).

**One-offs are small and disclosed.** One-off tax benefits of ₹138.8 cr in FY23 and ₹36.0 cr in FY25 (prior-year tax); no exceptional items in FY26 or Q1FY27. Our forward P/E median on EPS before them is 89.6x vs 88.4x reported: immaterial.

**Other income is small and falling.** FY26 ₹74.1 cr (interest on deposits ₹54.0 cr, FX ₹6.7 cr, rent ₹5.3 cr, gains on investments ₹4.1 cr), down from ₹124.3 cr as cash was spent. We forecast ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.1|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.2|num}} cr.

**Leases move costs below EBITDA.** Under Ind AS 116 rent on the 68 leased stores is depreciation and interest, not opex (lease interest ₹120.8 cr in FY26). As leasing rises, EBITDA flatters slightly; PBT is the fairer comparison (CFO, 28-Jul-2026).
**Employee stock options** cost ₹33.9 cr in FY26, charged to the P&L; dilution is ~0.2% a year (promoters 74.65% to 74.48% since Jun-2025).
**Tax** is ~25% on the store business and ~27% consolidated because DMart Ready's losses earn no tax credit.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Unqualified audit by S R B C & Co (EY network), a simple single-segment business, full standalone and subsidiary disclosure, small related-party flows. Watch inventory days (up to ~33 from ~29) and the growing lease book.

sections.title: No longer net cash: ₹965 cr of commercial paper and ₹1,460 cr of leases against ₹308 cr of cash at Mar-26

blocks.p: Until FY25 DMart carried no debt apart from leases. In FY26 it issued commercial paper and short-term loans (₹965 cr at Mar-26) and lease liabilities rose to ₹1,460 cr (₹820 cr) as more stores were leased; cash, bank deposits and investments fell to ₹308 cr. Net debt is ₹657 cr before leases and ₹2,117 cr including them: tiny against ₹24,464 cr of equity and ~₹5,200 cr of EBITDA (debt/equity 0.09x). Inventory is the main working-capital item: ₹5,901 cr (~37 days), up as more distribution centres opened; DMart pays suppliers in ~8 days on purpose, buying better prices with its own cash. Contingent liabilities are ₹437 cr, mostly indirect-tax disputes.

sections.title: The street after Q1: mostly Hold, targets ₹3,700-4,700, median ₹4,058

blocks.p: After the Q1FY27 results (11-Jul-2026) and the analyst meet (28-Jul) the street moved to the middle. Motilal Oswal downgraded to Neutral with ₹4,015 (35x Sep-28E pre-Ind AS EV/EBITDA, ~60x P/E), from Buy at ₹4,800 two weeks earlier; HDFC Securities kept Add at ₹4,100 (DCF, ~58x Jun-28E P/E); Prabhudas Lilladher Hold at ₹4,000 (DCF; ~65x FY28E); Nuvama Hold at ₹4,383 (from ₹4,974); Emkay Sell at ₹3,700 (DCF, ~54x FY28E standalone EPS); Elara Accumulate at ₹4,700. Median of the six: ₹4,058, +7% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹3,801. No single method: JM uses P/E (65x Mar-28E); HSIE, PL and Emkay use DCF but state the implied one-year-forward P/E (58x, ~65x, 54x); MOSL uses EV/EBITDA and states the implied P/E (~60x Sep-28E). P/E on one-year-forward EPS is the common language, so it is our primary method; EV/EBITDA and DCF are cross-checks.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a great business at a full price; HOLD

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's lowest-cost large grocery retailer, run by a disciplined, owner-aligned team, adding ~15% more stores a year with a 2-3 year land pipeline and a margin it will not chase. Growth has slowed to ~15% as same-store sales fade in crowded metros (quick commerce takes the small baskets) and new stores in smaller towns ramp slowly. Capital needs are rising: capex is above operating cash, borrowings are back and ROE is ~13%. The online arm loses ~₹300 cr a year.

**What you are paying:** 74.7x our FY27E and 63.5x FY28E EPS. DMart's own forward P/E has a median of 88.4x since 2021; listed retailers were 30.2% below their five-year medians on 30-Sep-2026, which gives 61.5x Sep-28E EPS and {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD on our rule. EV/EBITDA (₹3,657) is a little below; a DCF at an 11% cost of capital (₹989) is far below.

bullets: **Rating: HOLD, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.

**We would turn BUY below ~₹3,515** and SELL above ~₹4,255 on today's numbers; we would raise the target if like-for-like growth recovers towards 8-10% with openings on plan, and cut it if LFL stays near 5% and openings slip.
**This is mainly a multiple call.** Our Sep-28E EPS (₹65.7) is a little below the street; our 61.5x sits inside the 54-65x the street's targets imply. The post-Q1 street median is ₹4,058.
**Biggest swing factor:** the multiple. Each 5x of P/E is ~₹330 a share; each 1% of revenue per sq ft is ~₹0.8 of FY28E EPS.

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Everyday low cost / everyday low price: keep costs low and pass the savings to customers as permanently low prices instead of promotions.
Like-for-like (same-store) sales growth: revenue growth of stores open for at least 24 months.
Selling space in DMart stores, in million sq ft; "effective" area in our model weights stores by the part of the year they were open.
General merchandise and apparel: kitchenware, plastics, home textiles, toys, garments and footwear.
Delivery of groceries in 10-30 minutes from small "dark stores" (Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto, Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now).
DMart's online grocery service (Avenue E-Commerce), delivering large baskets within six hours.
Avenue Supermarts alone (the stores) / the group including DMart Ready and other subsidiaries.
Accounting rule that puts leased stores on the balance sheet; rent becomes depreciation plus interest.
Short-term (under one year) borrowing / non-convertible debentures (longer-term bonds).
Share price ÷ earnings per share; enterprise value (market value plus net debt) ÷ EBITDA.
Half of FY28E plus half of FY29E: the 12-month-forward earnings the market will look at in September 2027.
How far comparable stocks trade below their own five-year median P/E on the valuation date.
Discounted cash flow valuation; the cost of capital is the required annual return used to discount future cash.
Return on equity (profit ÷ net worth) / return on capital employed (operating profit ÷ debt plus equity).
